items.title: OpenAI announces three big science discoveries and a new way to work with academics
items.summary: Less than a month after its mass release of hundreds of manuscripts that it said contained solutions to long-standing mathematics questions, OpenAI is back with three more "major" discoveries in math, computer science, and physics. What's different this time is the choice to have
items.content:
This time OpenAI says it’s taking new advice from scientists on how to release the results.

Less than a month after its mass release of hundreds of manuscripts that it said contained solutions to long-standing mathematics questions, OpenAI is back with three more “major” discoveries in math, computer science, and physics . What’s different this time is the choice to have external experts that OpenAI describes as “shepherds” guiding the results in computer science and physics, while for the math problem it says that they advised it to release the AI output for researchers to work through their own explanations.

OpenAI results added to GitHub today:

Local smoothing for the Euclidean wave equation. The proof uses an auxiliary partial differential equation to establish Sogge’s local smoothing for waves in every spatial dimension at least two. It also yields the Kakeya maximal and dimension conjectures and Stein’s spherical restriction estimates throughout the interior of the conjectured range. We are releasing the model output directly, as we did in our October 6 release.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False. The paper gives a deterministic algorithm that exactly counts satisfying assignments of fixed-width CNF formulas in subexponential time and polynomial space. The case of 3-SAT refutes the Exponential Time Hypothesis. An independent working group of computer scientists led by Russell Impagliazzo, Ramamohan Paturi, and Ryan Williams will examine and explain the proof. At the group’s request, we are making the materials public immediately so others can examine them as well.

This approach could have its own issues, the company admits, and the AGMAI panel of math advisers OpenAI put together just said yesterday that “we recommend that AI companies do not adopt” the practices of designating certain people to receive the output first, citing unequal access, borrowed reputation, and biased selection as a few of the issues. Instead, they recommended that in the future, AI labs release output on scholarly repositories, with Lean-formalized proofs, info on how the problems were chosen, funding for people working on understanding the results, and other information.

The physics information has not been released in full, but is a “mathematically rigorous existence proof of certain interacting quantum field theories containing gauge fields and fermions in four dimensions, including Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and a unified completion of the Standard Model of particle physics.” According to OpenAI, “David Gross will lead a group including Michael Douglas, Arthur Jaffe, Igor Klebanov, and Nikita Nekrasov that will shepherd this work.”

The computer science collaboration is said to prove that the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) , which has been widely believed to be true, is actually false. OpenAI says verification of the result will be guided by a group of three experts that includes UC San Diego’s Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, who were part of the group that originally proposed it in 1999 , as well as MIT professor Ryan Williams . The group decided to release the AI output write-up and Lean proof on GitHub today .

They also released an open letter to the community asking for input on how to examine the claim, and about setting norms for dealing with AI-generated breakthroughs:

We would welcome discussion of three broader questions:

What expectations should govern early access to AI-generated results, disclosure of conflicts of interest, and the use of unpublished material for subsequent research?

How should credit recognize both new discoveries and the work of checking, fixing, simplifying, explaining, and extending them?

How can we support students and researchers as methods and research directions change, while preserving the understanding and judgment needed to question results and develop new ideas?

There’s similar documentation for the math breakthrough, where its model “produced a proof of the local smoothing conjecture in every dimension and therefore also resolve the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture in all dimensions.” Just a few months ago, NYU professor Hong Wang was awarded a prestigious Fields Medal by the International Mathematical Union for resolving the Kakeya conjecture in three dimensions.

Grok Says Its AI-Generated Version of ‘The Odyssey’ Is ‘Not Historically Accurate’
items.summary: Months after Elon Musk declared that the xAI model would outclass Christopher Nolan’s mythological epic, the bot itself admitted defeat.
items.content:
You don’t hear the defenders of so-called western civilization talk much about The Odyssey these days.

Maybe that’s because their rabid denunciations of Christopher Nolan’s film adaptation of Homer’s epic were buried in an avalanche of money. The July blockbuster has grossed nearly $1.8 billion worldwide, silencing the right-wingers who predicted a massive flop due to diverse casting and deviations from the source material.

Perhaps the loudest of these preemptive critics was Elon Musk. The world’s richest man spared no vitriol for what he considered a desecration of the ancient Greek narrative; four days after its release, he vowed to produce a superior version. “Before this year ends,” Musk wrote on X, “Grok Imagine will make a full-length movie of The Odyssey that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer.”

A little more than three months later—long after the discourse moved on—the public finally has a first glimpse of what we might call the Grodyssey , an Odyssey rendered through prompts fed into xAI’s video and image generation model. Rather than a “full-length movie,” it’s a seven-minute “episode” of an apparently ongoing series, depicting how Odysseus, King of Ithaca, resists a call to war against Troy but is ultimately compelled by an oath of loyalty to sail there with his army.

“Odyssey with Grok Imagine,” Musk announced Friday on X when sharing the clip, produced by AI entertainment company Wonder Studios X. The subdued post received just 18,000 likes, notably less engagement than other recent posts in which Musk cast doubt on the results of Brazil’s elections, complained about pronouns, and disparaged “legacy news.”

Grok’s introductory episode bears many hallmarks of AI slop. The movements of faces don’t match the dialogue, which is further undercut by stilted and unnatural delivery. Besides Odysseus, none of the principal characters are introduced by name, and the pacing issues are laughable: the Ithacans arrive on the shores of Troy immediately after leaving their homeland, for example. Even the blue checks on X were harsh in their assessment. “Someone actually watched this and still decided to post it?” wrote one user . “Fire that person.”

But Musk’s stated goal wasn’t to deliver a better-looking or more narratively cohesive version of The Odyssey . He and his culture war comrades dubiously claimed that they were against Nolan’s casting of Black and trans actors, the Americanized English spoken by the characters they played, and various designs of ships and armor in the film because they were “historically inaccurate.” Hence Musk’s guarantee of a “historically accurate” corrective.

So, did Grok Imagine succeed on that front? Asking Grok for a self-evaluation yields an interesting answer. “No,” the chatbot says when queried about whether this Odyssey snippet is historically accurate. “Grok Imagine’s Episode 1 (and the broader promised series) is an adaptation of Homer’s Odyssey , not a historically accurate reconstruction of real events.”

The AI model further notes that the characters have no basis in the historical record, and that the poem is dominated by “myth” and “invention” rather than confirmed events. “Homeric society mixes possible Bronze Age elements (palace-centered kingdoms, certain warrior practices) with later Iron Age features,” it also states. “Many details are anachronistic or literary.”

In laying out the reasons that the episode “does not meet a strict historical standard,” Grok points out that the characters speak modern English with British accents, “not Homeric Greek or any reconstructed Bronze Age language.” Visually, it says, the production reflects “modern cinematic tropes and AI training data,” not “primary archaeological evidence.” (The bot cites the appearance of cavalry in a battle scene as an error when compared with standard reconstructions of the period.) Grok concludes that “ The Odyssey itself is not a historical document, and the production makes no serious attempt at archaeological or linguistic fidelity beyond a general ‘ancient Greek epic’ aesthetic.”

Of course, the creative license that comes with adapting a millennia-old legend swarming with gods, witches, magic, and monsters was understood by just about everyone but Musk and a handful of cranks insisting that Nolan had contradicted some fundamentally true account of heroic adventure. Even Grok can tell you that its master’s fit of pique led him to promise the impossible—as he so often does .

items.title: Microsoft offers to buy out a quarter of its workforce
items.summary: Employees in the US, Canada, India, and the UK may receive offers to leave MS today.
items.content:
On Monday, Microsoft said it will offer voluntary buyouts to eligible employees in select parts of the company. CNBC reports that the buyouts will be offered to roughly 60,000 employees , or about a quarter of its global workforce. The company describes the offer as an opportunity for employees who may have already been considering career moves outside Microsoft. While Microsoft did not give a direct reason for the buyout package, it comes as the company has spent the last several years managing costs amid investment in AI infrastructure and data-center buildout.

Microsoft will extend the voluntary exit offer (VEO) to qualifying employees in the United States, India, Canada, and the United Kingdom. Microsoft employees at level 70 or below will be eligible for the buyout program. The company’s employee rankings are internal, but according to the salary and career database Levels.fyi , levels 65–67 correspond to principal positions, and 68–70 are at the partner/distinguished level. According to Chief People Officer Amy Coleman, eligible organizations were selected “based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs.”

The effort is the second time Microsoft has run a voluntary workforce reduction in 2026. In April, the company offered its first voluntary retirement package to 8,750 US employees. In July, the Xbox division laid off 3,200 employees , or about 20 percent of its entire gaming division. As reported by CNBC , about 30 percent of eligible employees accepted the retirement offer, lessening the impact of the planned layoffs, according to Coleman. While the offer in April went out to long-tenured employees who might be nearing the end of their career, the VEO expands the effort to a much larger potential pool.

In comments to GeekWire in July, Coleman said Microsoft was looking into making voluntary exits part of workforce management more regularly. She described the current VEO as something that “builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program.”

While layoffs remain the most common way to reduce headcounts in the tech world, Microsoft may be following Google’s playbook. As Business Insider reported, Alphabet offered employees voluntary exit packages in June and October 2025, and again in February 2026. Now, eligible Microsoft employees may have to decide whether to take a deal now or keep their jobs and face the uncertainty of future company-wide layoffs.

According to Microsoft’s blog , employees eligible for the VEO will be contacted via email on Monday. Microsoft will announce its latest earnings after market close later this week.

items.title: Anthropic is burning gas to feed the AI boom
items.summary: As it prepares to go public, Anthropic's S-1 filing makes generative AI's methane dependency glaringly obvious. "Competition for access to electrical supply and data center locations with adequate power availability is intense." In documents filed with the US Securities and Excha
items.content:
Anthropic is clear that data centers will run on gas, to the company’s own detriment.

As it prepares to go public , Anthropic’s S-1 filing makes generative AI’s methane dependency glaringly obvious.

“Competition for access to electrical supply and data center locations with adequate power availability is intense.”

In documents filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission Monday, Anthropic acknowledges that data centers are becoming increasingly reliant on “natural gas” — the fossil fuel industry’s marketing term for what is primarily methane — leaving the company’s AI data center buildout vulnerable to rising fuel costs and existing supply chain constraints. And in a possible catch-22, Anthropic admits that rising global temperatures — a symptom of burning fossil fuels — will increase the company’s operating costs.

“Competition for access to electrical supply and data center locations with adequate power availability is intense,” Anthropic says, adding that some of its planned data centers rely on electricity generated by natural gas turbines on-site. Anthropic leases capacity from hyperscalers, but it announced a $50 billion dollar plan last year to expand data centers in Texas and New York.

The US, the epicenter for data centers globally, is planning to build more fossil fuel generation capacity than it has in a decade as data centers demand more electricity. Donald Trump’s administration has sought to kill renewable energy projects while tilting the regulatory landscape in favor of fossil fuels , which Trump claims is a more important energy source for powering data centers around the clock than solar and wind farms that generate power intermittently.

Now, a shortage of gas turbines is slowing data center construction . Some developers are installing gas engines on-site as a way to avoid long wait times to connect to power grids. Developers are also turning to more simple turbine technology at these sites as they face backlogs from turbine manufacturers, making on-site power generation less efficient and more polluting as a result.

Data center electricity demand could wipe out decades of gains in air quality over the next five years, one recent Texas-based study found — raising levels of soot, smog-forming pollutants, and planet-heating carbon dioxide. Even as data centers create more greenhouse gas pollution, Anthropic’s S-1 points to climate change as a risk to its bottom line. It will have to pay more for electricity and water to cool servers at data centers as temperatures climb.

Nevertheless, Anthropic expects increased competition for natural gas and pipeline capacity from hyperscalers and cloud service providers rushing to build their own data centers. “This competition could drive up the price of natural gas,” the company notes.

Gas makes up the biggest chunk of the US electricity mix, 40 percent of the nation’s power generation . And Americans are already feeling the pain of rising costs as utilities scramble to upgrade energy infrastructure and meet rising power demand.

Pissed-off residents have successfully blocked dozens of proposed data centers across the US . Anthropic acknowledges that the specter of ballooning utility bills is enough to interfere with a data center project. “If our efforts to secure electrical power are perceived to affect other utility customers and the broader grid, regulators may impose conditions, standby charges, or other requirements intended to address such impacts,” it says.

If regulators push data center developers to shoulder more of the costs for new energy infrastructure, Anthropic says that could also raise its operating costs. And without a secure gas supply and the pipelines to transport the fuel, the company says, it might need to delay or abandon planned data center projects altogether.

Ultimately, these challenges could stunt Anthropic’s growth:

Any failure to secure access to adequate electrical power, any legal, regulatory, or other administrative action or change limiting the availability of electricity, or any significant increase in energy or compliance costs, could adversely affect our cost structure and limit our ability to scale our compute infrastructure, develop and deploy our models, and service our customers.

items.title: Why Anthropic’s IPO Prospectus Is Missing So Many Key Figures
items.summary: Anthropic’s S-1 filing is hundreds of pages long—and it leaves out quite a few financial details. “Anthropic owes investors more information,” one analyst tells WIRED.
items.content:
Anthropic filed its hotly anticipated IPO prospectus on Monday, spelling out parts of the company’s business, strategy, and risk profile ahead of its public debut. Though the filing, known as an S-1, is several hundred pages long, it has some notable omissions—namely, certain financial figures.

“Claude has experienced the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, as demonstrated by revenue growing from $0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $_____ for the three months ended September 30, 2026,” reads the first of dozens of such examples.

It’s relatively common for companies to redact certain information in their S-1 filings, and Securities and Exchange Commission rules allow for a certain degree of leniency around the practice, particularly when it comes to information considered “confidential.”

Still, it’s helpful to know what, exactly, these companies decide to leave out. In Anthropic’s case, the missing details largely revolve around financials for its most recent quarter, which concluded at the end of September, and lease agreements tied to its compute investments. While experts expect many details to be disclosed before Anthropic goes public, their current absence may hint at the uncertainties of investing in artificial intelligence, as companies work to secure sufficient compute.

Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.

Michael Dambra, accounting and law professor at University at Buffalo School of Management, tells WIRED that there are “practical reasons” for its third quarter numbers to be absent: September 30 was only a few weeks ago, and “closing the books for a company of this size takes time.”

Companies can also be liable for misstatements in their registration statements, “so there is a strong incentive not to publish numbers before they have been fully vetted,” Dambra says. SEC rules require that “Anthropic would need to update the filing with third-quarter financials” if the company goes public any later than about mid-November, he says.

As for data center lease agreements, Erica Neuman, an accounting professor at Youngstown State University, says it’s “not unusual” for companies to redact confidential details from “contract exhibits,” which could include lease terms .

However, Neuman adds that it’s worth scrutinizing whether Anthropic’s redactions would prevent, or make it more difficult, for investors to analyze Anthropic’s financial obligations and whether they may impact the company’s cash flow.

Many of Anthropic’s financial obligations relate to compute, which is the “most significant operating cost in our business,” according to the S-1. It’s also a business risk for the company, and it’s laid out both in terms of undersupply and overinvestment. (Parts of the AI industry have been warning that chip constraints could slow the progress of AI.)

Anthropic’s prospectus puts more emphasis on the risks of overinvestment, stating that the company needs to make forward investments in compute resources that will seem “irresponsibly large” at first glance.

Chips, Anthropic explains, are approached as a “single, fungible pool from multiple strategic partners,” including Amazon, Google, Nvidia, and AMD. The company notes that it has entered into contracts “with an aggregate committed spend of more than $____, substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure.” Some of these contracts are set to be completed before December of 2030, while others may extend through 2045.

Though the prospectus touches on Anthropic’s compute uncertainties due to factors like limited land and power resources, Patrick Moorhead, CEO and chief analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy believes investors are owed more detail.

“It’s about characterizing the odds and impact individually across each of the areas. Anthropic owes investors more information, such as a probability of these individual issues, characterizing the percentage chance and the degree of the impact,” he tells WIRED. “Not ‘could materially impact.’”

Anthropic does provide some eye-catching estimates in footnotes. Since December 31, 2025, it has started or amended “compute and infrastructure” leases with “future minimum payment obligations” worth approximately $417 billion in aggregate. Since June 30, it’s added another $245 billion to its future payment obligations, all related to infrastructure agreements. It also expanded “certain existing commercial agreements” that it caveats “have not yet been finalized,” for an additional $125 billion to $150 billion.

Include “short term” agreements with “minimum non-cancelable payments,” Anthropic says, and that’s another $21 billion. In total, it will owe, at minimum, an estimated $808 billion if it follows through on all of this.

Ben Bajarin, chief executive and a principal analyst at Creative Strategies who tracks the chip industry, says that this is likely just the first draft of Anthropic’s prospectus, and that he expects a lot of gaps to be filled in an updated version.

Despite how common S-1 redactions are, Dambra describes them as “controversial.” While companies may argue that they’re “protecting proprietary information,” Dambra says that skeptics accuse them of using redactions “opportunistically” in order to “avoid disclosing politically or socially sensitive information.”

However, Dambra argues that redacting information may come at a cost. He notes that companies with redactions in their S-1s were also more likely to “underprice” their shares at the initial public offering.

When companies redact information in their S-1, Dambra says they typically understand that they’ve created an “information gap” between them and outside investors. Understanding that investors will treat this gap with “suspicion,” companies may feel inclined to “entice” them to participate in the IPO by setting a lower starting price.

items.title: Apple releases iOS and macOS 27.2 with new Siri AI features, new Music logo
items.summary: Included is the ability to limit which applications Siri can directly access.
items.content:
Today, Apple rolled out the 27.2 updates for its operating systems, including iOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, visionOS, and so on.

Let’s start with iOS 27.2. This update is heavily focused on Siri AI. It adds a memory feature to Siri, so it can “recall your past conversations” and reference them when chatting with you. It also expands what data sources Siri can access when giving responses to include voicemails, Messages attachments, and more.

On the flip side, there is now an “Excluded Apps” option that allows you to “choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access.” Further, Siri AI is now available in five more languages beyond English, as previously announced: French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish—though Siri AI remains unavailable in Europe (and mainland China).

Other additions include context-aware suggestions within Messages (like turning a message inviting you to something into a calendar entry), SynthID watermarking support in Photos, and support for user profiles in the Apple TV app. There’s also the new Apple Music branding , plus the arrival of previously promised Apple Pencil support on the iPhone Duo foldable.

The macOS Golden Gate 27.2 offers some of the same things: contextual memory for Siri, the same additional Siri AI languages, and miscellaneous unspecified bug fixes. The same goes for the Apple Watch—again, mostly the same Siri-related updates. visionOS 27.2 includes the new languages and updated Music icon, as well.

Also, as previously discovered in the beta releases of macOS 27.2, there are some references to new gesture recognition capabilities in applications like Photos, Notes, and Safari—which may be related to unconfirmed reports of touch support on the next MacBook Pro refresh, which may be revealed at a scheduled public briefing this Wednesday.

Apple’s own iOS and macOS update notes are below.

Siri AI (All iPhone 16 models and later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max)

This update provides enhancements to Siri AI with the ability to retain useful context from previous Siri interactions as well as draw from a wider range of personal context. It also introduces Suggestions in Messages that help you take quick actions in apps like Calendar and Reminders based on context from your conversation. This release includes additional features, bug fixes, and security updates for your Mac.

items.title: Uh-oh, it sounds like the iPhone Duo keeps cracking and users aren’t happy about it
items.summary: A small number of early adopters of the much-hyped new foldable phone from Apple have complained of screens cracking.
items.content:
The launch of the iPhone Duo , Apple’s hotly anticipated foldable phone, is off to a rough start. The phone was announced at this year’s Surprise and Shine event, with Apple promising that it had finally gotten a notoriously tricky form factor right.

Now, however, Bloomberg reports that early Duo users have been complaining about screens cracking “after just hours or days of use.” Some users have reported hearing a loud crunching noise, followed by the appearance of a crack. Others have reported display malfunctions.

404 Media has also reported that early adopters are dealing with “big fat creases down the middle of the [$2,000] folding screen.”

TechCrunch reached out to Apple for comment and will update this story if it responds. The company told Bloomberg that it was “aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units.”

Creating a functional foldable phone has long been an ambition in Silicon Valley, but many of the models released so far have suffered from similar maladies . Apple promised that it had cracked the code, but these early complaints suggest it may not have solved the problem after all.

items.title: Apple reveals updated iPad mini with a bigger OLED screen for $700
items.summary: Apple claims this is the most significant update ever for the iPad mini line.
items.content:
The iPhone Duo may be a bit of a risk right now , but there’s a new mid-size Apple touchscreen device that might do the job. Starting at $699, the 8th-gen iPad mini price has gone up, but there are some big changes. Apple says the refreshed 8th-gen iPad mini marks the most significant update ever for its petite tablet, featuring an OLED screen and the A20 Pro chip that we first saw in the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo.

The new iPad mini has roughly the same footprint as the 2024 release, but the display is slightly larger thanks to a 24 percent reduction in bezel thickness. The device is almost a full millimeter thinner than the last iPad, coming in at just 5.4 mm. The chassis is also IP67 rated for water and dust protection. The 7th-Gen iPad mini didn’t have any official IP rating.

The 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR display (up from 8.3 inches) moves on from the IPS technology of the last-gen device to adopt OLED. That means dapper blacks and a much higher peak brightness—1,200 nits versus just 500 nits for the previous mini. It can also manage 1-nit minimum brightness so as not to sear your retinas in a dark room. There will also be a nano-textured matte display option. The display experience on the new mini should be much more in line with what we’ve come to expect from Apple’s Pro-level devices.

Credit: Apple Credit: Apple

The 2-nanometer A20 Pro chip was a noticeable upgrade in the iPhone 18 Pro , and it will be even more significant in this tablet. The previous model had a 3-nanometer A17 Pro chip, which was already a year old when it appeared in the iPad mini. In the iPhone 18 Pro, we found the A20 Pro significantly improved graphics performance thanks in part to a 50 percent increase in memory bandwidth.

Higher memory speed also helps with on-device AI applications, but the Neural Engine is the primary factor. Unfortunately, not all versions of the new iPad mini will be equally capable. Apple notes the 512GB configuration will have the dual 16-core Neural Engine we saw in the iPhone 18 Pro, but the 128GB and 256GB versions will have a single 16-core NPU. These versions will also have a slightly different CPU configuration, with five cores instead of six.

Apple has retained the 12 MP cameras for the front and back of the tablet, but the front-facing one has changed location. Rather than being on the short edge for portrait-orientation video calls, it’s now on the long edge. That might take a little getting used to for those who frequently use their tablets for FaceTime.

The $699 base price gets you 128GB of storage and Wi-Fi connectivity. It’s $100 more for 256GB and $300 more for 512GB. The nano-texture display is also a $100 upsell, but it’s only available for the 256GB and 512GB versions. The step up to cellular will cost $849 for the 128GB model.

Pricing is, sadly, not eye-popping for 2026, but it marks yet another price increase for Apple. The 7th-gen iPad mini launched for $499 in 2024, but it has since risen to $599. The new model adds $100, but it does have some nice upgrades. Preorders for the new iPad mini begin at 10:10 am PT on October 28 (Wednesday), and devices will arrive on doorsteps and in stores on November 6.

items.title: ICE plan to buy robot dogs spurs protest from hundreds of Boston Dynamics employees
items.summary: US robotics company stands by ICE deal as more than 300 employees warn of risk.
items.content:
Hundreds of employees at the US robotics firm Boston Dynamics signed a petition calling for executives to halt a sale of the company’s robot dogs to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement—but executives stood by the deal, while saying the robots would not be weaponized.

On September 25, the Department of Homeland Security contract awarded $1.3 million to a Connecticut company called Radeco to provide ICE with modified versions of Boston Dynamics’ quadruped robots. But Boston Dynamics workers sent the petition letter with more than 300 signatures—half of them anonymous—to the company’s executives in early September and shared copies with The Boston Globe and WBUR public radio station .

“Many of us have gotten messages from friends and family, asking us in disbelief and horror if this news is true, and how we can live with ourselves if it is,” according to the petition. “The risk for Boston Dynamics is simply too great to continue with this deal.”

The petition described the signatories as employees who normally “love showing off what we do to our friends, family and the world” and who “love challenging ourselves to innovate and change the perception of what robots can do.” The 300 signatures come out of a total Boston Dynamics workforce of approximately 1,400 people.

The ICE contract covers the purchase of four Boston Dynamics Spot robots that were modified by Radeco to be marketed as a robot platform named Cerberus . The contract describes these Cerberus robots as being intended to “detect radiation, toxic gas leaks and explosive threats in urban environments or disaster zones,” along with enabling other remote observation and inspection missions.

A centerpiece of the upgraded robot is an oxygen sensor that is intended to “ensure the air quality is breathable when personnel are placed in confined spaces such as tunnels.” The Cerberus robot dog also has a camera equipped with 30-times zoom capability, 360-degree cameras, and infrared thermal imaging.

The Cerberus robot dog would come with an optional Spot robotic arm that enables it to manipulate objects and open doors, along with providing additional camera views when extended. The ICE contract describes the robot as being generally capable of navigating complex industrial environments on its own and executing “repeatable autonomous missions with minimal human intervention.”

Such a purchase was justified in the ICE contract as supporting the Homeland Security Task Forces’ mission to carry out “counter-illicit cross-border tunnel operations” and dismantling “cross-border human smuggling and trafficking networks” being conducted by “criminal cartels, foreign gangs and transnational criminal organizations throughout the United States.”

“Spot robots are tools that help keep people out of harm’s way,” a Boston Dynamics spokesperson told Ars in a statement. “Regardless of any political implications or personal feelings about the organizations involved, if our robot can help keep people safe, we believe it should.”

Boston Dynamics has also emphasized that the robots would primarily be used by ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations unit that is focused on combating transnational criminal organizations, according to WBUR.

However, the Brennan Center for Justice has documented the Homeland Security Investigations unit as frequently being involved in deporting undocumented workers and conducting workplace raids during the first administration of President Donald Trump. These operations occurred between 2018 and 2021, before being halted by US Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas early in the term of President Joe Biden.

During Trump’s second term that began in January 2025, the Homeland Security Investigations unit once again diverted thousands of agents to immigration enforcement and deportations after one of Trump’s executive orders redefined the unit’s primary mission, according to the Immigration Policy Tracking Project .

The Boston Dynamics employee petition specifically referenced an ICE and Homeland Security Investigations workplace raid that detained 475 primarily South Korean workers at the Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America facility in Georgia on September 4, 2025. Hyundai Motor Group became the parent company of Boston Dynamics after acquiring the US robotics company in June 2021.

“We cannot be proud of working at Boston Dynamics when that work is being used by a government agency that brutalizes civilians, including some of our own colleagues at Hyundai,” according to the employee petition. “All elements of the ICE organization, not just Enforcement & Removal Operations, have worked to sow fear among all people living in this country.”

That single largest immigration enforcement operation of its kind sparked public outrage in South Korea and led to South Korean leaders questioning the country’s business investments in the United States. However, Hyundai has maintained its operations at the US electric vehicle production at the Metaplant America factory and still plans to deploy thousands of Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid robots starting at its US facilities.

The Boston Dynamics leadership team has stood by the ICE contract with Radeco, which would mainly involve Boston Dynamics providing technical support for the modified robots, according to The Boston Globe.

The company also responded to the employee petition via an email from Amanda McMaster, former interim CEO for Boston Dynamics. That email was obtained and quoted in part by both The Boston Globe and WBUR.

“We believe this decision is in line with our purpose of ethically advancing intelligent machines in service of humanity,” McMaster wrote in her email. She urged workers to “respect and accept this decision, even if you do not agree with it.”

items.title: Type Server Protocol
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.com/microsoft/pylance-release/blob/main/docs/tsp/type-server-protocol.md Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50248371 Points: 248 # Comments: 166
items.content:
The Type Server Protocol (TSP) is a JSON-RPC protocol for asking a type server for Python analysis data. A type server maintains the type-analysis state for a workspace and answers requests for the protocol version, snapshots, Python search paths, import resolution, and type queries (computed, declared, and expected types).

The protocol uses Language Server Protocol (LSP) data shapes and conventions where they are useful, such as Position and Range , and it represents URIs as strings the same way LSP does. TSP methods use the typeServer/ prefix.

The protocol artifacts in this folder are the authoritative definitions:

TSP uses semantic version strings for client/server compatibility checks. While the protocol is in the 0.x line, minor version changes may be breaking. Patch version changes remain backward compatible within the same minor line.

A client starts a type server and communicates with it over the main JSON-RPC connection using a transport the server supports, such as stdio or Node IPC. When using stdio, stdout must be reserved for JSON-RPC protocol messages.

A type server is expected to receive enough workspace and document state to answer the TSP requests it supports. Clients commonly use normal LSP initialization and document synchronization for this state, then send typeServer/* requests on the same JSON-RPC connection.

TSP also supports optional extra read-only connections. The original connection remains the main connection and owns initialization, workspace state, document synchronization, state-changing notifications, and connection control. Extra connections are opened only after client and server negotiate support during initialization.

A typical session follows this order:

Multi-connection mode is an optional performance feature. It lets a client open additional local channels to the same type server for read-only TSP requests, while the main connection continues to own the mutable workspace state.

Clients should use multi-connection mode only when they can benefit from concurrent read-only work, such as high-volume type queries or background workers that should not block the main JSON-RPC connection. A server must still work correctly in single-connection mode. Multi-connection support must not be required for protocol correctness.

Multi-connection support is negotiated through the normal LSP initialize request and response. A client that can open extra TSP channels advertises the supported transport kinds under capabilities.experimental.typeServerMultiConnection :

A server that can serve extra TSP channels returns the same capability shape in the initialize result:

Multi-connection mode is enabled only when both sides advertise typeServerMultiConnection and the two supportedTransports lists have at least one transport in common. If either side omits the capability, or if there is no common transport, the session remains single-connection and the client must not send typeServer/connection .

The currently supported built-in transport kind for extra connections is ipc . This negotiation is separate from the main connection, which can use stdio or Node IPC.

After initialization and transport negotiation, the client opens an extra channel by sending typeServer/connection on the main connection:

For ipc , the args array identifies the endpoint or endpoints that the server should connect to. The server should validate the request, connect to the supplied endpoint promptly, and return a result with success: true when it accepts the request. If the server cannot open the channel, it should return success: false and include a short message when useful for logs.

An ipc endpoint is expected to provide a full-duplex JSON-RPC stream when the platform IPC mechanism supports it. In that case, args contains one endpoint string:

If the platform IPC mechanism exposes only one-way endpoints, args contains two endpoint strings. The endpoint names are from the type server's perspective: the first endpoint is the server input stream, and the second endpoint is the server output stream.

The client closes an extra channel by sending typeServer/connection on the main connection with the same transport kind and endpoint identity:

The server should stop serving the matching extra channel and close the transport promptly. A client may also tear down its local transport if the server does not complete the close within the client's timeout budget.

The close request should use the same args shape that opened the channel: one endpoint for a full-duplex IPC stream, or the same input/output endpoint pair for a split IPC stream.

The main connection owns all state-changing traffic. The following must remain main-connection-only:

Extra connections are TSP-only and read-only. They may be used for requests that do not mutate server state and whose results are valid for the snapshot supplied by the client.

The allowed TSP messages on an extra connection are bound to the negotiated TSP version. If a server reports support for a TSP version and advertises multi-connection support for that session, it must support every extra-connection TSP message defined for that version.

The table below lists the TSP version that first allows each message on an extra connection:

Servers should reject LSP traffic, state-changing notifications, typeServer/connection , and any TSP message not allowed for the negotiated TSP version when received on an extra connection.

A snapshot is a non-negative integer that identifies a point-in-time view of the type server's analysis state. Type handles, declarations, symbols, and other returned objects are valid only for the snapshot in which they were returned unless a request explicitly says otherwise.

items.title: Oldest GUI application that still runs on Windows 11
items.summary: Article URL: https://blog.enlyth.com/posts/oldest-windows-gui-app-win-11/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50248055 Points: 449 # Comments: 259
items.content:
For a while I’ve been wondering about a silly question, which is, what’s the oldest application with a GUI that will still run on Windows 11 without modifications or emulation.

Given Windows’ excellent backwards compatibility, I expected the answer to be something impressively old.

Sadly, Windows 11 can’t run 16-bit Windows programs by itself, because 64-bit Windows has no NTVDM , so we’re going to have to find something from the early NT era.

I remember asking this question a while ago on an anonymous forum, where someone pointed me to Win32s , and suggested to find an early release version of it with FREECELL.exe .

So I did exactly that, and lo and behold, FREECELL.EXE with a date modified of 22-Feb-93 running and fully playable, without any changes on the latest version of Windows 11:

At the time of this post, that’s a 33 years and 8 months old application, which is impressively almost as old as me.

So I kinda thought “cool”, considered this a solved mystery and forgot about it shortly afterwards. But for some reason, this question popped into my mind again lately and this time I decided to dig deeper to see if I can find something older.

Digging through old Windows versions on the Internet Archive, I found some early NT 3.1 pre-release versions that seemed promising, but the main issue seemed to be either incompatibility with today’s executable format or API changes that came later in development.

The earliest 1991 versions used a draft PE format not compatible with modern Windows, and builds up to mid-1992 assumed the cdecl calling convention instead of stdcall for Windows API calls, so arguments would get removed twice, as such:

Which would understandably cause the program to crash.

There was one application that caught my eye though, from Build 347, and that was CDPLAYER.EXE , linked on 16-Nov-1992 . By then the calling convention was fixed, but the other programs in that build crash in their bundled C runtime. CDPLAYER.EXE avoids that by using the system’s crtdll.dll , and Windows 11 still ships a crtdll.dll in SysWOW64 .

If you start the program, you get something like this:

That is because, duh, my computer doesn’t have a CD-ROM drive. But you can use a small DLL ( cdemu.dll ) to emulate one with some fake audio data and actually get it to play audio:

Pretty cool for a program that’s almost 34 years old!

So earlier I mentioned that 16-bit programs are out of the picture because they are no longer supported.

But if you want, you can use something like otvdm to run older Windows applications.

Behold, a fully playable version of REVERSI.EXE dated 15-Nov-1985 running on Windows 11, taken from Windows 1.01:

And although using otvdm does feel like cheating, I thought it was cool enough to include in this post.

items.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here. After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus. The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays
items.content:
After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus. The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and the ways it believes it will change the world.

But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years. In fact, its public messaging is a master class in narrative capture.

Earlier this month, Jack Clark, the company’s cofounder and head of policy, gave a speech at the IMF meeting in Bangkok in which he announced to the assembled economists, bankers, and lawmakers that the singularity is already here.

Introduced by the science fiction writer and futurist Vernor Vinge around 40 years ago (and long debated on the nerdier fringes of the internet), the singularity is supposed to be the point at which technology gets so good that it outstrips the abilities of its makers.

Humans are left in the dust, the idea goes, no longer able to compete with—or even understand—the fruits of their former creation.

And this fictional world that many of us have imagined since we were kids? Apparently we’re already living in it: “I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun,” Clark told his audience.

The company tells a vivid (and in many ways scary) story about a future it portrays as inevitable but one that has not yet happened, often co-opted from well-worn science fiction memes. It presents its technology as mysterious and dangerous, and insists that it is the only company trustworthy enough to tame it. (What investor wouldn’t want in on that?)

Take another example. Last year, Chris Olah, another Anthropic cofounder, was invited to address the Vatican, where he told Pope Leo XIV and other religious scholars and officials what his company was learning about its technology. “I will be honest: We keep finding things that are mysterious, even unsettling,” he said. “We find evidence of introspection. We find internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease.”

Never mind that many researchers would scoff at such an overt suggestion that Anthropic’s software has humanlike inner experience. When so little seems certain, what Anthropic (and its fellow frontier AI companies) say is snatched up and clung to like pieces of a sinking ship.

I’m not saying they’re necessarily wrong about any of this. (That’s for another day.) But in a world where nobody knows what’s coming, companies like Anthropic get to fill the vacuum.

It’s worth taking a moment to ask: What is Anthropic? It might sound like a starter question on a family quiz show, but it’s far harder to answer than you might think.

The question has been on my mind since reading an exchange on X last week kicked off by Nathan Calvin, who is chief strategy officer at Encode AI, an organization based in Washington, DC, that advocates for regulation. Calvin was unhappy about the legislation that Anthropic proposed in a draft bill it circulated in secret to US lawmakers (which was then leaked ).

Anthropic wants to be seen as the good guy, Calvin said. But why should we trust it? “What is Anthropic?” he asked.

Here’s one answer: Anthropic is a company whose IPO values it at more than $1.5 trillion, netting its cofounders, including Clark and Olah, vast wealth.

But Anthropic has always insisted it is more than that. As Calvin noted: Anthropic might instead be considered an AI safety organization focused on developing powerful technology that is reliable and (almost) risk-free. Or it might be considered a group of people hell-bent on creating a technology with superhuman capabilities before anyone else—maybe because they believe they’re the most responsible people to do so, or maybe because of their egos.

In fact, Anthropic is all of these things. As CEO Dario Amodei put it in a reply to Calvin’s post : “Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the ‘race to the top’—by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.”

Amodei makes it sound as if he’s got it all tied up, but playing multiple roles is hard. There are huge tensions between the priorities of an AI safety organization and a profit-driven megacorp, for example. (Amodei admits in his post that he has made mistakes.)

Ultimately, the stories Anthropic tells itself should help us understand the stories it tells us. They should help us figure out how much to trust it to self-regulate or whether we should be forcing it to give external safety testers access to its models on our terms rather than theirs. They should help us give it the benefit of the doubt (or not) when what looks like a self-serving piece of legislation comes to light.

But I think the stories reveal a multiheaded hydra. Anthropic is many things to many people, and I’m not sure that makes it more trustworthy. In many ways, a good old-fashioned technology company—without the science fiction role-play, without the woo-woo—would be far easier to read.

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny.

items.title: This startup’s self-driving excavators help dig up $600M in new funding
items.summary: Bedrock Robotics, which is now valued at $4.1 billion, is particularly focused on autonomous excavators, in part because of a growing shortage of skilled operators.
items.content:
Bedrock Robotics has raised $600 million in a funding round that values the autonomous vehicle technology startup at $4.1 billion, marking a speedy ascent for the two-year-old company.

The Series C round, co-led by CapitalG and Emergence Capital, comes two months after the startup reached a key milestone: moving its autonomous excavators beyond testing and pilot programs and putting them to work on active construction sites.

Bedrock Robotics has developed a self-driving kit that can be retrofitted onto construction and other worksite vehicles. Excavators outfitted with Bedrock’s autonomous-driving tech are now commercially operating at a Nevada-based water treatment facility, an earthwork site run by Champion Site Prep in Texas , and a 1.2 million-cubic-yard civil sitework project with Zachry Construction Corporation.

Bedrock has raised nearly $1 billion since it was founded in 2024 by a group of autonomous vehicle and robotics industry veterans. Co-founder and CEO Boris Sofman previously led Waymo’s now-shuttered self-driving trucks program. Sofman also co-founded and led Anki Robotics, the maker of the popular Cozmo consumer robot, which shut down in 2019.

Other co-founders include Waymo veterans Kevin Peterson, Bedrock’s chief technology officer, and Ajay Gummalla, who serves as Bedrock’s vice president of engineering and infrastructure. Tom Eliaz, who previously worked at Segment and Twilio, is also a co-founder and VP of engineering and hardware.

The fresh capital will help Bedrock accelerate its transition to commercial work. The company plans to deploy its technology at more construction sites, while expanding the teams and infrastructure needed to support customers in the field.

“We have proven that fully autonomous excavators can perform real work of value alongside the crews and workflows already in place on job sites. The next challenge is delivering that capability to more contractors as a dependable part of how projects get built,” Sofman said in a statement.

Bedrock is particularly focused on autonomous excavators, in part because of a growing shortage of skilled operators. It takes five years or more to master operating an excavator, according to Bedrock. Meanwhile, a growing number of construction workers are approaching retirement age. The Associated Builders and Contractors, a national construction industry trade association, estimates that more than 40% of construction workers will retire in the next five years.

Bedrock is betting that the industry will increasingly turn to autonomous driving tech to help close that labor gap.

The startup’s newest partner is Haydon, an Arizona-based general contractor that plans to use Bedrock-equipped machines across a range of projects, including advanced manufacturing facilities, water and wastewater plants, data centers, and healthcare facilities.

New investors US Innovative Technology Fund (USIT), Bessemer Venture Partners, and Temasek participated in the round, alongside existing investors 8VC, Georgian, Valor Equity Partners, Xora, Eclipse, Perry Creek Capital, and Nvidia.

The startup also announced two executive hires as it scales commercial operations. Amy Jones Satrom, a veteran of Amazon, Nuro, and Uber, has joined Bedrock as its vice president of operations. Lando Juarez, formerly head of legal for Uber’s autonomous mobility and delivery business, was hired as general counsel.

items.title: The RealReal won’t let AI agents hog designer clothing
items.summary: The RealReal, a secondhand luxury fashion consignment retailer, said it's updating its bot defense system, effectively making it harder for AI agents to shop on its site. The change comes days after The Verge reported that an AI agent could be used to take advantage of The RealRe
items.content:
Previous reporting by The Verge found that Meta’s Muse could be used to effectively block other shoppers from purchasing items for hours.﻿

The RealReal, a secondhand luxury fashion consignment retailer, said it’s updating its bot defense system, effectively making it harder for AI agents to shop on its site.

The change comes days after The Verge reported that an AI agent could be used to take advantage of The RealReal’s item reserve system. On the retailer’s website, an item goes “on hold” and is unavailable for other customers to buy for 20 minutes once it’s placed in a user’s shopping cart. Using Meta’s Muse, The Verge was able to instruct the AI agent to continuously re-add The RealReal listings in a shopping cart as soon as the 20-minute hold had expired, effectively blocking other shoppers from purchasing products for hours or longer.

After publication, chief technology officer Luke Friang said in an email that the company had addressed the Muse use case flagged by The Verge ’s story. The RealReal’s bot defense configuration now makes it much more difficult for all agents to log in, add items to cart, and check out, Friang said. Agents will still be able to surface listings from The RealReal and direct Muse users to product pages, Friang said, adding that the company will continue to strengthen protections as AI-powered online shopping evolves.

Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Technology companies are selling agents as personalized assistants for billions of people — always-on, compliant entities that will schedule meetings, throw parties, and purchase things for human users. So far, agents and shopping seem to go hand in hand; Meta said in its Q3 earnings call this month that it was the most common use case for Muse so far, and that purchases were over $200 on average. Muse has been a hit for Meta and could signal a turning point for AI agents: The company said 10 million people in the US had downloaded the app in 40 days.

But robots shopping for things instead of humans has the potential to upend the balance of the web as we know it. For one, if humans stop visiting websites directly and instead access the web through chatbots, businesses become one step removed from their customers. Retailers — most notably Amazon — have recognized that reality could disrupt their bottom line, especially advertising revenue, and have blocked agents from shopping on their sites.

An influx of AI agents accessing consumer platforms could also break or complicate even the most unexpected things shoppers take for granted, like the reserve system of a used clothing website. There is, of course, a realistic limit to how long a person is willing to spend adding and re-adding designer clothing to their shopping cart if they’re indecisive. An agent in contrast does not care. It is perhaps precisely the type of busywork a fashion-forward person might pay an actual personal assistant to do on their behalf. Now, a capability like this is at the fingertips of millions of consumers, and they are just beginning to learn how to take advantage of it. Retailers, too, are playing catch-up.

items.title: Apple acknowledges iPhone Duo display ‘issue’ after reports of cracked screens
items.summary: Following reports of iPhone Duos with cracked and broken inside screens, often showing a bright line running from the center to the right side, Apple says in a statement to Bloomberg and 9to5Mac that it's aware of "an issue impacting the inner display" on a "small number of iPhon
items.content:
Apple says a ‘small number’ of iPhone Duos have shown the cracked inner screen problem and that owners should contact AppleCare.

Following reports of iPhone Duos with cracked and broken inside screens, often showing a bright line running from the center to the right side, Apple says in a statement to Bloomberg and 9to5Mac that it’s aware of “an issue impacting the inner display” on a “small number of iPhone Duo units.” If your iPhone Duo is affected, Apple says to contact AppleCare for a replacement.

Here is the full statement, which Apple’s Alex Kirschner shared with The Verge :

The response to iPhone Duo from early users has been incredibly positive, and we are seeing exciting things from developers who are rapidly updating their apps to take advantage of its unique form factor. We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units. If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement.

Kirshner says most units aren’t susceptible and that the issues appear quickly on units with the defect.

Shortly after launch, iPhone Duo users started reporting similar issues where the hinge would tighten, and opening the device caused a crack and the distinctive bright lines on the display. One user in Australia said that an Apple Store replaced their unit “on the spot.”

This weekend, iFixit published its teardown of the phone and gave its perspective on why some phones might be cracking. Where the damage has been happening, iFixit shows how the foldable screen might be pushing against a center bar.

The Verge has contacted Apple about the reports, but has not received an on-the-record response about the issues with these new phones. They’re some of the first devices to launch after new CEO John Ternus took over from Tim Cook .

items.title: Some iPhone Duo screens are already failing
items.summary: Apple's "precision-engineered" hinge is apparently damaging some iPhone Duo screens.
items.content:
The iPhone Duo launched last week, offering anyone willing to spend $2,000 a chance to experience Apple’s first foldable phone. For some early buyers, the morning after isn’t going great. Despite the company’s big talk about its “precision-engineered” hinge, some devices appear to have a hardware flaw that destroys the device’s impressive internal display within hours (or minutes) of use.

The Internet is currently overflowing with images of busted iPhone Duos, all sporting almost identical damage. The OLED is marred by several bright lines originating just below the midpoint of the display. These bands of damaged pixels extend all the way to the bottom and right edges. Some units also show lines of dead pixels following the crease from the top to the area where the bright lines begin.

Anyone who has seen a damaged OLED panel will be familiar with this type of defect. When the layers of the display are damaged, the pixels no longer receive the correct voltage to illuminate them. Instead, they get the full driving voltage and are permanently on at maximum brightness. Some pixels can get no voltage, leaving them totally black. The only fix is to replace the OLED, but swapping the iPhone Duo’s screen reportedly costs half as much as the device itself.

It sounds like most affected devices are failing within about a day of use. But a few unlucky buyers note they only opened and closed the phone a few times , and in some cases, they hadn’t even finished the initial setup process. Some customers have reported success taking their defective phones to Apple stores for replacement, but spares may be in short supply right now.

In the absence of any official explanation, iFixit may be the next best thing. The site has already torn an iPhone Duo apart and taken a close look at the affected area. After years of seeing other foldables fail, there are a few suspects to check. Since foldables need to pass data and power across the hinge, there’s always a cable tucked in there that could press on the screen. The iPhone Duo has a wide cable with “accordion-like pleats,” according to iFixit, but this doesn’t quite match the accounts of the damage.

People with broken $2,000 iPhones say there’s unusual physical resistance and sometimes even a clicking sound as the device closes. After that, the lines appear. Using CT scans of the phone, iFixit has shown that the point of failure starts below where the ribbon cable passes through the hinge. The width of the supporting hinge mechanism changes in that spot, suggesting a mechanical misalignment.

The animation above shows iFixit’s best guess at what’s happening. The support bar in that narrowed section of the hinge may be getting stuck, preventing it from dropping far enough to accommodate the waterdrop bend in the OLED panel when the device closes. This creates stress on the display that ultimately damages the matrix. YouTuber CuriousHagi also zeroed in on that region, identifying a place where the thinner link may be snapping during operation. He speculates the component is physically sticking to the support plate.

If this fiddly little hinge piece is the culprit, there’s no way to prevent the OLED on an affected device from failing. It could happen after five minutes or five days, but continuous pressure on an OLED panel will eventually lead to permanent damage.

Apple has yet to acknowledge the issue, and it probably won’t have anything to say until the problem is fully investigated. The scale is impossible to know—Apple sells a lot of devices, so even a low failure rate could see a flood of reports on social media. Adding moving parts to a phone will lead to at least some increase in hardware issues. Apple certainly wouldn’t be the first device maker to have problems with its first foldable launch.

In 2019, Samsung released the original Galaxy Fold with a much more primitive hinge design. Even before launch, reviewers began seeing OLED damage after a few days of use. The issue in that case was a design with openings that allowed particulates to infiltrate the hinge , where they damaged the screen from underneath. Samsung delayed the release while it re-engineered the hinge.

Samsung’s foldables have not been bulletproof by any means, but there have not been widespread reports of defects immediately after unboxing. Other makers of foldable phones move so few units that occasional defects may not make waves online. Apple is just lucky that way.

items.title: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals its strategy for keeping enterprise customers hooked
items.summary: Anthropic’s S-1 shows more than half of its $100,000-plus customers now use both the Claude Platform and a first-party app, a cross-selling playbook reminiscent of Amazon that’s making enterprise customers stickier.
items.content:
Anthropic is building the same kind of cross-product ecosystem that helped make tech companies like Amazon and Uber enormously sticky, and its S-1 suggests the strategy is working. More than half of customers spending at least $100,000 annually now use both the Claude platform and a first-party app like Claude Code or Cowork, up from about 30% at the end of last year.

“The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of AI,” the S-1, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday , reads.

As of September 30, Anthropic recorded more than 11,900 customers spending at least $100,000; more than 1,900 customers spending upwards of $1 million; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more annually.

Anthropic attributes customer momentum to a “significant usage expansion as customers realize the value of deploying Claude across their organizations,” which drove net revenue retention of about 900% as of the end of the third quarter.

Throwing shade at the entire legacy SaaS industry, Anthropic pitches Claude as not a “static product that serves a single use case,” but rather “frontier AI with rapidly advancing capabilities” spanning the models, the developer platform, and the applications users interact with directly.

“An advance at any layer compounds across all three layers, accelerating the pace at which we can deliver more capable intelligence,” the filing reads, calling this “integrated approach” the reason more customers use both the Claude Platform and first-party apps.

The playbook is familiar. Uber began by selling rides, but has expanded into food delivery and freight. With AWS, Amazon drew in customers with cloud computing services before expanding those relationships into storage, databases, and other offerings, making the ecosystem increasingly hard to leave. Like those companies, Anthropic doesn’t have to sell each product to a brand-new buyer: A business that starts with the API can deploy Claude Code to their engineers, and then Cowork to their broader workforce.

Those app users become far more valuable. In the third quarter, the highest-spending 5% of Claude Enterprise customers who used Claude Code spent about 20 times as much per month as the average enterprise user who didn’t use the coding tool, per the filing. The finding demonstrates how much room there is for per-user spend to grow, and illustrates why Anthropic is keen to get its applications into the accounts that start with the API.

Anthropic said it amplifies that organic diffusion by investing in Applied AI teams. An internal Applied AI team works with startups and enterprises to help place Claude inside customers’ existing technology stacks, and the company recently launched a separate venture with Blackstone and other private equity firms, dubbed Ode with Anthropic, to embed forward deployed engineers into businesses to build bespoke AI tools with Claude.

Anthropic also leans on its third-party distribution partnerships with hyperscalers AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Under what the filing calls a “joint go-to-market approach,” Anthropic holds the direct contractual relationship with customers and pays each cloud provider a fee, which the company says lets it “avoid channel conflict” and “set pricing.”

Anthropic’s budding stickiness strategy may become essential as the AI giant seeks to constantly “reinvent our business” by releasing “new classes of products whose aim is to dwarf the economic value of our existing ones.” The company says it will devote less effort than a typical business to “entrenching our current products and business models, and more effort to defining new ones.”

The filing also flags headwinds, despite impressive revenue growth of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. The cloud partnerships that help sell Claude are increasingly seeing Anthropic as a competitor, which Anthropic says could lead to difficulties securing the compute it needs from them. The filing states that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft may prioritize their own requirements or rivals they’ve invested in.

Customer concentration is another risk.

“Any adverse change in demand from our largest customers…could adversely affect our business and prospects,” reads part of the risk factors section. “As a result, a significant reduction in spending by, or the loss of, one or more of our largest customers, if not offset by new customer relationships or increased business from our other existing customers, could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.”

Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

items.title: SpaceX locks in $40B GPU financing deal with Apollo
items.summary: The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets.
items.content:
SpaceX has reached a binding commitment for roughly $40 billion in financing for AI chips and related data center equipment, the company disclosed in a regulatory filing Monday . SpaceX called the deal the “largest committed GPU financing” in a statement.

Under the agreement, an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, the New York-based private equity giant, will buy the chips and related server hardware, then lease the equipment to SpaceX. The leases will last about five to five-and-a-quarter years, beginning when each tranche of equipment is delivered, according to the filing.

SpaceX expects the deal to close by year-end, subject to closing conditions, with leases starting in the first half of 2027 as the GPUs and related equipment arrive.

The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets.

“This lease diversifies our funding sources and addresses a notable portion of the funding required to deliver on our growth plans,” SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said in a statement Monday, noting it is seeing “less than one-year payback periods” on its AI infrastructure investments as it scales compute to power Grok and its cloud services.

Apollo said the financing will help deliver Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX’s “terrestrial compute buildout.”

The financing comes as SpaceX ramps spending to expand its AI infrastructure, alongside its Starlink and launch businesses.

The financing follows a blockbuster third quarter for SpaceX’s AI business . SpaceX’s AI segment, which includes the Grok chatbot, the Cursor coding tool and its cloud compute business, outperformed investor expectations in the third quarter and brought in $7.6 billion of SpaceX’s $14.6 billion in revenue, more than Starlink and rocket launches combined.

Capital expenditures also surged to nearly $20 billion, up from $6.9 billion a year earlier, as SpaceX races to expand its compute footprint. CFO Bret Johnsen said on the company’s Oct. 20 earnings call that SpaceX expects to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter alone.

The massive lease comes after a tumultuous stretch in the debt markets for AI infrastructure players, as investors grow squeamish over runaway capital expenditures and limited profits.

While SpaceX had no trouble tapping Wall Street, Musk used the $40 billion announcement to take a victory lap over pure-play AI compute rivals.

Pointing to SpaceX’s “investment-grade” status and steady cash flow from Starlink and rocket launches, Musk argued on Sunday that debt markets have largely closed the door on companies without major revenue streams outside of AI data centers — spelling trouble for the more than 200 neocloud companies built solely to rent out GPUs for AI workloads.

“That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation,” Musk wrote on X. “Some will make it through, but not many.”

items.title: Microsoft offers buyouts to around 60,000 employees
items.summary: The buyout offers mark Microsoft's latest efforts to cut costs and rework its workforce.
items.content:
Microsoft is offering buyouts to around 60,000 employees, the company confirmed to TechCrunch on Monday. The move marks Microsoft’s latest efforts to cut costs and rework its workforce for the AI age.

Microsoft’s chief people officer, Amy Coleman, sent employees a note about the buyouts, which was also published on the company’s website.

Employees at the vice president level and below on select teams in the United States, Canada, India, and the United Kingdom will be eligible, according to the note. Bloomberg reports that divisions including Xbox, Windows, Copilot, and Finance are participating in the buyout offer. Some employees, including those working in data centers, sales and marketing, are excluded.

The news was first reported by Business Insider .

“The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter,” the note to employees reads. “This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support.”

The company said eligible employees would be receiving an email with a link to their Voluntary Exit Offer details on Monday. The terms of the buyout will be similar to Microsoft’s standard severance.

“The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us,” the note reads. “We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft. There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee. These are a few of the ways we’re trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute.”

The buyout offer gives Microsoft a way to reduce its workforce without resorting to the more disruptive approach of mass layoffs. It’s also not the first time that the company has offered buyouts. Earlier this year, Microsoft offered buyouts to retirement-age employees, with more than 30% of the roughly 8,750 eligible workers accepting.

Microsoft’s headcount as of the end of June was 223,000.
